paragraphs: Friend, look at what one man with one ram's horn can do. Sheba blows it, shouts, and "all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri" (2 Samuel 20:1-2). The people had just been through Absalom's rebellion, and they were still raw. Hurt and angry hearts are easy to follow a loud voice, and I think that's the warning here: be careful who you follow when everybody's upset.

Now look at the other voice in this story. Joab walks up to Amasa saying, "Are you well, my brother?" while a dagger is already out (2 Samuel 20:9-10). That's a friendly face with a heart that wasn't friendly. Then comes a wise woman in Abel-beth-maacah, a woman nobody expected, and she says "Why would you swallow up the LORD's inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). Her wise counsel did what a battering wall couldn't (2 Samuel 20:22). A whole army was pounding on the wall, and one calm voice settled it with a conversation.

So here's my big idea, baker. Don't just follow the loudest voice or trust the friendliest face. Ask who is really speaking, and what they're really after. Pray for wisdom like that woman had, because wise words can save a whole city. This is the last passage in Absalom's story, and what it shows is a kingdom still broken by people and still needing the Lord's wisdom.
